t.1.78.1: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: But having heard that a boy had been born, Devayānī of the bright smile, afflicted with sorrow, brooded about Śarmiṣṭhā, O Bhārata.
t.1.78.2: Approaching Śarmiṣṭhā, Devayānī said this: "What is this wrong you have done, fair-browed one, overcome by desire?"
t.1.78.3: A certain seer came here, righteous in spirit and versed in the Vedas; that granter of boons was asked by me for a wish in keeping with dharma.
t.1.78.4: I do not pursue desire unlawfully, O you of bright smile; my child is from that ṛṣi, and I tell you this truly.
t.1.78.5: That is well, timid one, if it is true; but is that brahmin known? I wish to know that brahmin by his gotra, his name, and his family.
t.1.78.6: Seeing him blazing with vigor and splendor like the sun, I had no power to question him, O you of pure smiles.
t.1.78.7: If this is so, Śarmiṣṭhā, I bear no anger, if indeed you have obtained offspring from a brahmin who is eldest and most excellent.
t.1.78.9: King Yayāti begot on Devayānī two sons, Yadu and Turvasu, who were like a second Śakra and Viṣṇu.
t.1.78.8: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having spoken thus to each other and laughed together, the two women parted, and the Bhārgavī went home, believing it to be simply the truth.
t.1.78.10: And from that same royal sage, Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan, bore three sons: Druhyu, Anu, and Pūru.
t.1.78.11: Then, at a certain time, O king, Devayānī of the bright smile went out into the great forest together with Yayāti.
t.1.78.12: And then she saw there boys with the forms of gods, playing quite at ease, and, astonished, she said this:
t.1.78.14: Having thus questioned the king, she then asked the boys: "Little sons, what is the name and the lineage of your father, the brahmin? Tell me truly, for I wish to hear of him."
t.1.78.13: Whose are these handsome boys, O king, who are like the sons of gods? In splendor and in form they seem to me to resemble you.
t.1.78.16: Having spoken thus, they approached the king together; but the king, being then in the presence of Devayānī, did not welcome them. Then the boys, weeping, went to Śarmiṣṭhā.
t.1.78.17: But having seen the affection of those boys toward the king, and having understood the truth of the matter, the queen spoke these words to Śarmiṣṭhā.
t.1.78.15: With their forefingers the boys pointed to that very best of kings, and they also told him that Śarmiṣṭhā was their mother.
t.1.78.18: Though you are dependent on me, why have you done what is displeasing to me? Having taken up that very Asura way of conduct, are you not afraid?
t.1.78.20: When the king was chosen by you, he was at that very moment chosen by me as well; for a friend's husband, by dharma, becomes one's husband too, O lovely one.
t.1.78.19: What I said, that it was a ṛṣi, is true, O sweet-smiling one. Since I conduct myself according to propriety and according to dharma, I do not fear you.
t.1.78.21: You are worthy of my honor and respect, a brahmin woman, elder and most excellent; yet even more than you, the royal seer is most worthy of my honor. Do you not know that?
t.1.78.22: Then, having heard her words, Devayānī said this: "O king, I will not dwell here today; you have done what is displeasing to me."
t.1.78.24: The king, alarmed, followed close behind her, trying to soothe her; but she, her eyes red with anger, would not turn back.
t.1.78.23: Seeing her, the dark-complexioned lady, suddenly spring up with tear-filled eyes and set out swiftly toward Kāvya, he was then deeply troubled.
t.1.78.25: But the lovely-eyed one, saying nothing at all to the king, arrived, as if in no time, in the presence of Uśanas Kāvya.
t.1.78.26: But she, as soon as she saw her father, greeted him respectfully and stood before him; and immediately after, Yayāti paid homage to the Bhārgava.
t.1.78.27: Dharma has been conquered by adharma, and what was low has risen above the high. I have been outdone by Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan.
t.1.78.28: Three sons have been begotten on her by this king Yayāti, but I, ill-fated as I am, have only two sons, father, I tell you.
t.1.78.29: This king, renowned as one who knows dharma, has overstepped the bounds of propriety, O best of the Bhṛgus; this I tell you, O Kāvya.
t.1.78.30: Since you, great king, though knowing dharma, have done adharma as if it were pleasing, old age, hard to conquer, shall soon overpower you.
t.1.78.32: A man who, when chosen, does not grant the season to a woman who asks for it is called here a slayer of the embryo, O brahmin, by those who expound the Veda.
t.1.78.31: O blessed one, when the daughter of the lord of the Dānavas begged me for her season, I did this righteous deed with no other thought in mind.
t.1.78.33: But the man who, when entreated in private by a desirous woman who is lawfully approachable, does not go to her, is called by the wise, in matters of dharma, a slayer of the embryo.
t.1.78.34: Having considered these reasons, O best of the Bhṛgus, I, agitated by fear of unrighteousness, went to Śarmiṣṭhā.
t.1.78.36: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Yayāti Nāhuṣa, cursed by the enraged Uśanas, abandoned his former youth and at once fell into old age.
t.1.78.35: Surely I ought to have been consulted by you, for you are dependent on me, O king. For one who acts falsely in matters of dharma, it amounts to theft, O Nāhuṣa.
t.1.78.37: I am not yet sated with youth in Devayānī, O best of the Bhṛgus; show me your grace, O brahmin, so that this old age may not enter me.
t.1.78.38: I do not speak this falsely: you have attained old age, O lord of the earth. But if you wish, you may transfer this old age to another.
t.1.78.39: Yayāti said: "O Brahmin, that son who would give me his youth shall be the one to share in the kingdom, and likewise in merit and in fame; may you consent to that."
t.1.78.40: Śukra said: You shall transfer your old age as you wish, O son of Nahuṣa, by meditating on me with devotion, and you shall incur no sin.
t.1.78.41: That son of yours who gives you his youth shall become king, long-lived and renowned, and likewise blessed with many offspring.
